questions.stem: "FIFO" means:
options: the last item added is the first one removed
the first item added is the first one removed
items are removed in sorted order
questions.explanation: Last in, first out (a) is a stack — Week 6.

questions.stem: enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3), dequeue(), enqueue(4), dequeue(). What does the next dequeue() return?
questions.explanation: The queue goes [1, 2, 3] → dequeue 1 → [2, 3] → enqueue 4 → [2, 3, 4] → dequeue 2 → [3, 4]; the next dequeue returns 3. (A stack would have returned 4 — the difference in one question.)

questions.stem: In SlowQueue, dequeue is pop(0) on a DynamicArray. Its cost on a queue of n items is:
options: O(n) — every remaining element shifts one slot left
questions.explanation: pop(0) moves the n − 1 elements behind the front. Amortised O(1) (c) is the cost of append, the enqueue.

questions.stem: An array-based queue that enqueues with insert_at(0, x) and dequeues with pop() at the end has costs:
questions.explanation: pop() at the end moves nothing, but insert_at(0, x) shifts everything. With a plain array, whichever end is the front, one operation is O(n).

questions.stem: A CircularQueue with capacity 8 has head = 6 and size = 3. The next enqueue writes to slot:
questions.explanation: (6 + 3) % 8 = 9 % 8 = 1. Slot 9 (a) does not exist; the items are in slots 6, 7 and 0.

questions.stem: A CircularQueue with capacity 5 has head = 4 and size = 2. After one dequeue, head is:
questions.explanation: (4 + 1) % 5 = 0: the head wraps. Slot 5 (a) is past the end of the Array.

questions.stem: A ring buffer that stores only head and tail (no size) finds head == tail. The queue is:
options: either full or empty — it cannot tell which
questions.explanation: Empty: nothing between head and tail. Full: the tail has come all the way round to the head. Both look the same.

questions.stem: CircularQueue keeps a _size field because:
options: it tells a full ring from an empty one, which look the same by head and tail
len would otherwise be O(n) with no other benefit
the Array does not know its own length
questions.explanation: With the size, empty is size == 0 and full is size == capacity. The Array does know its length (c): len(block).

questions.stem: A full ring of capacity 4 holds [E, F, C, D] with head = 2. It grows to capacity 8 by copying new[i] = old[i] and keeping head = 2. Read front to back, the queue is now:
questions.explanation: Slots 2 and 3 of the new block hold C and D, slots 4 and 5 are empty, and E and F sit in slots 0 and 1 — behind the front. The correct copy gives (a) with head = 0.

questions.stem: A queue on a singly linked list with head and tail references should put the front of the queue at:
options: either end — it makes no difference
questions.explanation: Dequeue at the head (pop_front, O(1)), enqueue after the tail (O(1)).

questions.stem: Why not dequeue at the tail of a singly linked list?
options: Removing the last node needs the node before it, which takes an O(n) walk
The tail node has no value
It would make the queue LIFO
questions.explanation: The new tail is the node before the old one, and a singly linked list can only find it by walking from the head.

questions.stem: A queue built from two stacks (inbox and outbox, pouring only when outbox is empty): enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3), dequeue(). How many items are now in outbox?
questions.explanation: The first dequeue finds outbox empty and pours all three: outbox holds 3, 2, 1 (1 on top). It pops 1, leaving 2 and 3.

questions.stem: The cost of dequeue on that two-stack queue is:
options: amortised O(1) — each item is poured from inbox to outbox at most once
questions.explanation: One dequeue can pour n items, so the worst case (c) is O(n), but each item is pushed, poured and popped once in its life.

questions.stem: Which of these needs a queue?
questions.explanation: BFS visits nodes in the order they were discovered: FIFO. The other three are stack applications from Week 6.

questions.stem: n enqueues followed by n dequeues on a SlowQueue cost in total:
questions.explanation: Dequeue number i shifts n − i elements: (n-1) + (n-2) + … + 0 = n(n-1)/2.

questions.stem: In Python, (0 - 1) % 8 is:
questions.explanation: Python's % takes the sign of the divisor, so the result is in 0..7: stepping back from slot 0 wraps to slot 7. In C or Java the answer would be −1 (a).

questions.stem: A deque is a structure that:
options: serves the most urgent item first
can only be used as a stack
adds and removes at both ends
questions.explanation: A double-ended queue. (a) is a priority queue.

questions.stem: Measured, a ring-buffer dequeue and a linked-queue dequeue are both flat lines as n grows, but the ring is about five times slower. The reason:
options: a constant factor: the % and the bounds-checked Array access on every operation
the ring is really O(log n)
the ring copies the queue on every dequeue
the linked queue is O(1) and the ring is O(n)
questions.explanation: Both are O(1); the ring pays more per operation. Big-O hides constant factors, and measurement shows them.

questions.stem: Five people A, B, C, D, E stand in a circle; counting from A, every second person leaves. Who is left last?
questions.explanation: B, D, A and E leave in that order (W7-C2); C is last.

questions.stem: An array queue with a head index but no wrap-around, 8 slots: 8 enqueues, then 5 dequeues. How many more enqueues fit without growing the block?
questions.explanation: Tail = 8: there is no slot 8, even though slots 0 to 4 are dead and free. That is why the queue must wrap.

questions.stem: A CircularQueue that doubles its capacity when full has an enqueue cost of:
questions.explanation: The occasional copy is O(n), but doubling makes the copies total less than 2n over n enqueues — Lecture 04's argument.

questions.stem: A priority queue (Week 12) differs from a queue because it dequeues:
options: the most urgent item, not the oldest
questions.explanation: Same two operations, a different rule — and a different structure underneath, the heap.
